Learning Objectives
Review the basic science of articular cartilage.
Discuss blunt injuries to articular cartilage and recognize typical bone bruising patterns on
MRI.
Explain the classification of cartilage defects based on the International Cartilage Repair
Society classification system.
Describe important physical examination findings that guide the management of articular
cartilage defects.
List various surgical procedures for the management of articular cartilage defects.
Describe defect characteristics that help determine the appropriate surgical treatment option.
Define and review the etiology of osteochondritis dissecans.
Discuss the evaluation of patients in whom osteochondritis dissecans is suspected.

Review treatment options for osteochondritis dissecans lesions.
Basic Science of Articular Cartilage
Complex and highly organized structure
Primary component of articular cartilage is type II collagen.
Articular cartilage is aneural and lacks a blood supply, which contributes to its poor healing
potential.

Basic Science of Articular Cartilage
Articular cartilage is composed of type II hyaline cartilage that decreases force through
the joint by dissipating stress to the subchondral bone. Articular cartilage lacks a blood
supply, which is the reason it is unable self-repair after an injury. Injuries that penetrate
the subchondral bone (tidemark) may stimulate bone marrow content and growth
factors to the area of injury. This results in a fibrocartilage scar composed of type I
collagen, which lacks the mechanical strength of type II collagen.1
Blunt Articular Cartilage Injuries
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Blunt injury to articular cartilage likely occurs with most blunt trauma and ligamentous injuries
of the knee if excessive impact occurs.2
Blunt injuries cause impaction damage to the articular surface, which may consist of softening,
fibrillation, flap tears, cracking, or delamination.
Ligamentous injuries causing blunt injury frequently are associated with bone bruising.
Acute patellar dislocations also may result in blunt injury to the medial patellar facet and the
lateral femoral condyle.


Overview
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are notorious for blunt cartilage injuries and
bone bruising. Typical bone bruising patterns in ACL injuries include the middle third of
the lateral femoral condyle and the posterior third of the lateral tibial plateau (Figure 1).
Figure 1
Sagittal fat-suppressed MRI of a right knee obtained after anterior cruciate ligament
rupture shows a central femorla and a posterior lateral tibial plateau bone bruise. This
lateral pattern of injury is typical of that observed with the contact mechanism of injury.
(Reproduced with permission from Viskontas DG, Giuffre BM, Duggal N, Graham D,
Parker D, Coolican M: Bone bruises associated with ACL rupture: Correlation with injury
mechanism. Am J Sports Med 2008;36[5]:927-933.)
Acute patellar dislocations cause damage to the medial patellofemoral ligament and
blunt injury to the medial patellar facet and the lateral femoral condyle (Figure 2). In
addition, the image shows the patellar insertion, midsubstance, and femoral insertion of
the medial patellofemoral ligament.

Figure 2
T2-weighted axial MRI of a knee shows division of the medial patellofemoral ligament
into three regions: the femoral origin (FEM), midsubstance (MID), and patellar insertion
(PAT). The fibers of the medial patellofemoral ligament at the femoral and patellar
insertion sites are defined as normal, partially disrupted, or completely disrupted. This
image shows no injury to the medial patellofemoral ligament but shows medial patellar
facet and lateral femoral condyle contusions. (Reproduced with permission from Seeley
M, Bowman K, Walsh C, Sabb B, Vanderhave K: Magnetic resonance imaging of acute
patellar dislocation in children: Patterns of injury and risk factors for recurrence. J Pediatr
Orthop 2012;32[2]:145-155.)
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Blunt trauma can result in histologic, biochemical, and ultrastructural changes of the cartilage,
even in the absence of surface disruption.
Overt damage to the articular surface also may occur.
Injury Classification
The most widely used classification system is the modified Outerbridge classification system;
however, this classification system is outdated.
The ICRS classification system should be used to classify cartilage defects.


Injury Classification
The Outerbridge classification of cartilage defects is widely used; however, this
classification system is outdated. The ICRS system accounts for lesion size and depth.
Dwyer et al3 reported good interobserver and intraobserver reliability with the ICRS
classification system.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
The cause of full-thickness lesions may be acute injury or chronic repetitive overload.
Common mechanisms of injury include blunt trauma and shear stress.
Pathology is along a continuum ranging from contusion to fracture, ranging in depth from the
superficial articular cartilage to the underlying subchondral bone.
Most patients report pain.
Swelling is another common symptom.
Instability and mechanical symptoms also may be present.1
Physical Examination
Evaluate gait and alignment.
Determine if effusion is present.
Assess range of motion.
Determine if crepitus is present with motion.
Identify areas of tenderness, including joint line tenderness.
Evaluate for ligamentous injury.
Wilson test to detect potential osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) lesions
Internally rotate the tibia while extending the knee from 90° to 30°.
Positive if there pain is present with internal rotation and extension that is relieved with
external rotation
Imaging Studies

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may reveal articular cartilage damage.
T1- and T2-weighted MRIs can accentuate the evaluation of articular cartilage.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is first-line treatment.
This includes rest, anti-inflammatory medications, and activity modifications.
Steroids and viscosupplementation also can be used in patients older than 50 years.
Unloader braces can be used in patients with unicompartmental overload.

Nonsurgical Management
Because cartilage is aneural, most injuries result from repetitive microtrauma. Therefore,
a trial of nonsurgical management is important to determine that the cartilage injury is
the main source of symptoms. Physical therapy may be useful in patients with stiffness,
weakness, or poor neuromuscular control.
Surgical Management
Indications
Indications for surgical management are prolonged symptoms or overt damage to the articular
surface observed on imaging studies.
Techniques/Procedures
Arthroscopy can provide direct evaluation of cartilage damage.
Chondroplasty is indicated for the removal of unstable flaps and loose cartilage fragments.
Full-thickness lesions with exposed subchondral bone can be managed as outlined later in this
lesson.

Articular Cartilage Defects
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Articular cartilage injuries are common and may be idiopathic or associated with trauma.
Articular cartilage defects may be a challenge to manage because they have limited potential
for self-healing.

Overview
Articular cartilage and subchondral bone should be viewed as a single osteochondral
unit. Any disruption of this unit may lead to altered biomechanics and abnormal joint
contact pressures. Inflammation may occur as a result, leading to pain and altered
function.2
Epidemiology
Studies suggest the incidence of full-thickness cartilage lesions is between 5% and 10%.4,5
Chondral or osteochondral lesions can be found at the time of arthroscopy in more than 66%
of patients.
A recent review demonstrated that approximately 36% of athletes have focal chondral
defects.4

Epidemiology
The true prevalence of articular cartilage defects is difficult to determine because many
patients with these lesions are asymptomatic.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:24 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000531
7/38

The cause of full-thickness lesions may be acute injury or chronic repetitive overload.1
Common mechanisms of injury include blunt trauma and shear stress.
Pathology is along a continuum ranging from contusion to fracture, ranging in depth from the
superficial articular cartilage to the underlying subchondral bone.
Contact stress greater than 24 MPa is necessary to disrupt normal articular cartilage.
Although normal physical activity results in peak articular cartilage contact stresses of less
than 10 MPa, other factors, such as the rate of load and the effect of repetitive loading, are
important in articular cartilage injury.
If loading occurs too rapidly for fluid to shift in the matrix, high stress is generated, and
chondrocyte death and fissures can develop.
Articular cartilage fissures may be propagated by repetitive loading.
Associated Injuries
Articular cartilage injuries are associated with other intra-articular pathology, such as meniscal
tears, ACL tears, and patellar dislocations.
Chronic posterior cruciate ligament injuries may result in cartilage defects in the medial and
patellofemoral compartments.
They also may result from limb malalignment.
Injury Classification
Arthroscopy is the ideal method to evaluate articular cartilage in vivo; however, many
arthroscopic grading scales exist for articular cartilage of the knee.
The location, size, and severity of the lesion are important to determine.
The most widely used classification system is the modified Outerbridge classification system;
however, this classification system is outdated.
The ICRS classification system should be used to classify cartilage defects.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Most patients with symptomatic articular cartilage lesions report pain.
Swelling is a common symptom.
Instability and mechanical symptoms also may be present.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:24 AM
AAOS | Articular Cartilage Injury and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000531
8/38

A history of trauma may be reported; however, some patients may not recall any inciting
event.

Patient History
Pain with weight bearing is common in patients with symptomatic lesions. Patients
usually localize pain to the affected compartment.2
Physical Examination
A thorough clinical examination is critical.5
Evaluate gait and alignment.
Determine if effusion is present.
Assess range of motion and evaluate for any crepitus with motion.
Some patients with symptomatic articular cartilage lesions have tenderness over the involved
compartment.
Determine if any concomitant injuries may be present.
A thorough ligamentous examination is necessary.

Physical Examination
The clinical examination is an important component for diagnosis and ultimately may
guide management because some physical examination findings may be
contraindications to cartilage restoration. In addition, a good physical examination can
help determine if concomitant procedures are necessary. In evaluating a patient with an
articular cartilage injury, three key factors must be assessed.
Ligament status—Ligament insufficiency may negatively affect outcomes after
cartilage restoration procedures; therefore, surgeons must assess the integrity of
these ligaments.
Meniscal status—Absence of menisci increase joint contact forces twofold to
threefold. Meniscal repair or transplantation is considered, depending on tear type
and the quality of meniscal tissue.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:24 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000531
9/38

Patellofemoral and/or tibiofemoral alignment—Abnormal loads on the articular
surface may result from malalignment. Tibial tubercle, high tibial, or distal femoral
osteotomies may be performed in combination with a cartilage procedure depending
on lesion location.6
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs can underestimate isolated chondral lesions but may demonstrate joint space
narrowing, osteophytes, sclerosis, and cysts.
Weight-bearing AP and PA 45° flexion views allow for assessment of the joint space.
Lateral and sunrise/Merchant views are obtained to assess patellofemoral articulation.
Long-leg alignment views are used to determine the mechanical axis.

Radiography
Radiographs can be scrutinized for fractures, loose bodies, and joint space narrowing.
Full-length alignment radiographs should be obtained to evaluate the mechanical axis of
the limb (Figure 3). If malalignment is present, it should be addressed at the time of the
cartilage procedure.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000531
10/38

Figure 3
Full-length standing radiographs demonstrate varus (A) and valgus (B) malalignment. If
cartilage restoration procedures are indicated, malalignment should be addressed at the
same time as the cartilage restoration procedure or in a staged manner to improve
outcomes. (Reproduced from Mall NA, Harris JD, Cole BJ: Clinical evaluation and
preoperative planning of articular cartilage lesions of the knee. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2015;23[10]:633-640.)
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI can be performed to evaluate articular cartilage morphology and detect subchondral
edema.
It also can be performed to evaluate menisci and ligaments.
MRI underestimates cartilage lesion size by as much as 60% to 70% according to some
studies.2

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:24 AM
AAOS | Articular Cartilage Injury and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000531
11/38

MRI is a noninvasive imaging modality used to assess cartilage damage and potentially
guide management; however, MRI may not be the most reliable method to determine
cartilage defect size. A study by Campbell et al7 evaluated the efficacy of MRI in sizing
defects compared with arthroscopy. In 74% of lesions, the defect size was larger at the
time of surgery than that estimated via MRI. MRI undersized defects by a mean of 1.04
cm2. Although MRI is an excellent imaging modality for evaluating soft-tissue structures
in and about the knee, it may underestimate cartilage defect size, which may alter
treatment decisions.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Most articular cartilage lesions are initially managed nonsurgically.
This includes rest, anti-inflammatory medications, and activity modifications.
Steroids and viscosupplementation can be used but should be reserved for patients older than
55 years.
Unloader braces can be used in patients with unicompartmental overload.
Surgical ManagementIndications
Indications
Failed nonsurgical management
Symptomatic, focal, full-thickness cartilage lesions
Acute osteochondral lesions that can be fixed
Acute sheer forces with loose bodies
Acute patellar dislocation with loose body
Other pathology that may be contributing to the lesion is addressed or will be addressed as a
concomitant procedure. These include meniscal injury, ligament insufficiency, and
malalignment.
Techniques/Procedures
Lesion size and location and patient activity level must be considered in determining the
appropriate surgical procedure.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:24 AM
AAOS | Articular Cartilage Injury and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000531
12/38

Surgical treatment options can be categorized broadly as cartilage reparative marrow
stimulation techniques or restorative techniques.
Reparative marrow stimulation techniques initiate superclot formation, stem cell migration,
and eventual vascular ingrowth. They produce a fibrocartilage repair tissue that predominantly
contains type I collagen, whereas native hyaline cartilage primarily consists of type II collagen.
Marrow stimulation results in efflux of marrow elements into the defect, creating a superclot.
Microfracture is the most common marrow stimulation technique.
Cartilage restoration techniques fill the defect with hyaline cartilage via osteochondral plugs
(mosaicplasty) or via osteochondral allograft (OCA) transplantation.
Cell-based therapies involve the use of autologous chondrocytes to seed hyaluronan-based
scaffolds and tissue-engineered matrices for implantation into full-thickness defects.

Techniques/Procedures
A patient’s age, activity level, expectations, associated injuries, and defect size must be
considered in determining if surgical treatment is appropriate. The extensive
postoperative rehabilitation protocol should be discussed with the patient.2
Figure 4 shows a treatment algorithm for articular cartilage lesions in the knee. This
algorithm accounts for lesion size and location and patient activity level.6

Figure 4
Treatment algorithm for focal chondral lesions of the femoral condyle (left) and the
patellofemoral joint (right). Before management, surgeons must assess for correctable
lesions. Surgical management should be considered for trochlear and patellar lesions
only after rehabilitation programs have failed. The treatment decision is guided by the

on patient characteristics. (Reproduced from Cole BJ, Pascual-Garrido C, Grumet RC:
Surgical management of articular cartilage defects in the knee. Instr Course Lect
2010;59:181-204.)
Microfracture is a bone marrow stimulation technique used to manage full-thickness
cartilage defects. Microfracture can be performed via an arthroscopic, open, or mini-
open approach. Arthroscopic and mini-open techniques are most commonly used. The
first step in microfracture is to remove loose chondral flaps to create a contained defect
with stable borders of cartilage. The calcified cartilage layer is then removed, and the
subchondral bone is penetrated several times with the use of an awl or drill. This creates
an intralesional clot that leads to fibrocartilage tissue formation, which consists of type I

Osteochondral autograft transplantation (OAT) involves harvesting one or more
osteochondral plugs from an area of limited weight bearing on the femur for transfer to
the cartilage defect. This technique usually is performed in a mini-open fashion.
Arthroscopy is performed first to determine the size and shape of the defect. The defect
is prepared, and the femoral donor site is selected based on the characteristics of the
defect. The most common donor sites include the intercondylar notch and the
peripheral trochlea. A harvesting chisel is used to obtain the donor graft, which is then

with surrounding cartilage to minimize contact pressures. This provides hyaline cartilage
at the defect size, which is one of the main advantages of this technique (Figures 7 and
8). OAT typically is reserved for lesions smaller than 2 to 3 cm2.2

Large lesions (>2 to 3 cm2) or lesions with extensive subchondral bone involvement may
be managed via OCA transplantation. Fresh allografts are used to maintain chondrocyte
viability. This technique is similar to that for OAT; however, the allograft osteochondral
plug typically is larger. Ideally, the donor plug is harvested from a matching area on the
allograft to ensure appropriate contour (Figures 9 and 10).

The donor osteochondral cylinder is obtained from the fresh allograft specimen. D, The
donor cylindrical plug is inserted into the recipient tunnel using a press fit. (Reproduced
from Gomoll AH, Chilelli BJ: Articular cartilage of the knee, in Miller MD, ed: Orthopaedic

Video 2 shows the technique for OCA transplantation. Cell-based therapies typically are
used to managed defects 2 to 3 cm2 in size. These techniques involve the use of
autologous chondrocytes to produce hyaline-like cartilage. Cell-based techniques include
autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI) and matrix-induced ACI). ACI and matrix-
induced ACI are two-stage procedures, with the first stage consisting of arthroscopic
cartilage biopsy. Typical biopsy locations include the intercondylar notch or the
peripheral trochlea. Chondrocytes undergo in vitro expansion and then are reimplanted
into the defect as soon as 4 weeks after the initial surgical procedure; however, the cells
are kept frozen for 5 years, allowing ACI to potentially be performed years later. An
arthrotomy is performed to prepare the defect and create a stable border of
surrounding cartilage. For ACI, a synthetic collagen membrane is sutured in place, and
the cultured chondrocyte suspension is injected under the membrane with the use of an
angiocatheter (Figures 11 and 12). Matrix-induced ACI involves seeding a porcine type
I/type III collagen membrane with cultured chondrocytes, which is then secured to the
lesion with the use of fibrin glue.2 Video 3 shows this technique.

Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation protocols differ depending on the cartilage procedure performed.
Usually involves a period of restricted–weight bearing ranging from 4 to 8 weeks
Passive motion is encouraged, and a continuous passive motion device typically is used in the
early postoperative period.
Return to sports activity typically is delayed until 6 to 12 months postoperatively.
Outcomes
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:24 AM
AAOS | Articular Cartilage Injury and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000531
22/38

The management of full-thickness cartilage defects in the knee is an evolving area, with
evidence supporting marrow stimulation procedures, autologous osteochondral
transplantation, OCA transplantation, and ACI.

Outcomes
Various comparative outcome studies have assessed the outcomes of cartilage
procedures.
Mithoefer et al8 performed a systematic review to evaluate the clinical efficacy of
microfracture. Twenty-eight studies describing 3,122 patients were included in the
review. Mean follow-up in these studies was 41 months. Knee outcome scores improved
for the first 2 years after microfracture; however, insufficient data were available on
long-term outcomes.
Gudas et al9 performed a level I randomized controlled trial of 60 athletes, comparing
microfracture and OAT. After 37 months, patients in both groups had substantial clinical
improvement; however, patients treated via OAT had statistically significant better
outcome scores. In addition, 93% of patients who underwent OAT were able to return to
sports activity compared with 52% of patients who underwent microfracture.
Bentley et al10 performed a prospective randomized study of 100 patients with an
osteochondral defect and reported that 88% of the patients treated via ACI had good to
excellent outcome scores compared with 69% of the patients treated via OAT. The
patients were evaluated at 10-year follow-up, at which time graft failure had occurred in
17% of patients treated via ACI versus 55% of the patients treated via OAT.
DiBartola et al11 performed a systematic review on the clinical outcomes of ACI. Five
studies describing 115 patients who underwent ACI were included in the review. Mean
follow-up was 52.3 months, and mean defect size was 5.3 cm2. All studies showed
improvement in clinical outcome scores, with a mean increase of 35.7% in scores
postoperatively. Shorter duration of symptoms was found to potentially influence clinical
outcome.

Research has been conducted on the outcomes of OAT. Pareek et al12 performed a
systematic review on the efficacy of OAT. Ten studies with 610 patients were included,
with a mean follow-up of 10.2 years. International Knee Documentation Committee and
Lysholm Knee Scale scores improved by 42.4 and 21.1, respectively. The overall failure
rate was 28%, with a revision surgery rate of 19%. Older age, prior surgery, and defect
size correlated with an increased risk of failure.
Outcomes after OCA transplantation also have been studied. Assenmacher et al13
performed a systematic review on the outcomes of OCA. Five studies with 291 patients
were included, with a mean follow-up of 12.3 years. Clinical outcome scores substantially
improved postoperatively. The overall failure rate was 25% at 12.3 years; 72% of these
failures were conversions to total or unicompartmental arthroplasty. Patellofemoral
lesions were associated with poorer outcomes and a higher revision surgery rate.
Given the high rate of articular cartilage lesions in athletes, studies have been performed
to determine return-to-sport rates. A systematic review performed by Campbell et al14
included 20 studies and 1,117 patients. The return-to-sport rate was highest after OAT
(89%), followed by OCA transplantation, ACI, and microfracture (88%, 84%, and 75%,
respectively). Younger athletes with smaller lesions and a shorter duration of symptoms
had a better prognosis. Krych et al15 reported similar findings in a systematic. Return to
sports activity was highest after OAT (92%) followed by OCA transplantation, ACI, and
microfracture (88%, 82%, and 58%, respectively).
Osteochondritis Dissecans
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
OCD is focal idiopathic alteration of the subchondral bone with risk for instability and
disruption of the adjacent articular cartilage.
It may result in premature osteoarthritis.


Overview
OCD most commonly occurs in the femoral condyles of the knee; however, these lesions
also can occur in the elbow and talus.16
Epidemiology
The exact prevalence of OCD is unknown but has been estimated to be between 15 and 29 per
100,000 individuals.
OCD is more common in males, and bilateral lesions have been reported in as many as 25% of
patients.
In the knee, approximately 70% of OCD lesions are occur in the lateral aspect of the medial
femoral condyle, 15% to 20% occur in the central lateral femoral condyle, and 5% to 10% occur
in the patella. OCD lesions rarely affect the trochlea.
The most common location in the knee is the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle
(Figure 13).

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The cause of OCD is unknown. Repetitive trauma, ischemia, and genetics have been
implicated.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The exact etiology of OCD lesions is unknown. Several theories have suggested repetitive
trauma, ischemia, and genetics as the most likely causes. Repetitive stress is a popular
theory because most patients with OCD lesions are involved in sports. Despite the wide
acceptance of this theory, little evidence supports repetitive trauma as a cause. Loss of
blood flow has been theorized as a potential cause of OCD lesions. A lack of vascularity
has been postulated to inhibit the ability to reform new bone; however, little research
supports this theory. Despite the paucity of support, various treatment options,
including drilling, have been designed to improve vascularity. Some studies suggest
underlying genetic abnormalities as the cause of OCD lesions; however, no inheritance
patterns have been identified.17
Injury Classification
OCD lesions typically are classified as skeletally mature or immature, depending on the
maturity status of the distal femoral physis.
Various classification systems have been developed; however, no validated classification
system exists.

Injury Classification
Radiography, MRI, and arthroscopy have been incorporated to develop classification
systems. Plain radiographs do not adequately demonstrate disruption of the articular
surface or whether the lesion is attached to bone. MRI is much more accurate in
determining the stability of OCD lesions; however, no guidelines on the clinical utility of
MRI for diagnosis and staging exist. Arthroscopic evaluation provides excellent
visualization of the lesion and allows for thorough assessment of the stability of the OCD
lesion (Figure 14).

Patient History
Patients with OCD typically present with poorly localized knee pain, often without a history of
trauma or injury.
Pain often is associated with high activity levels and sports participation.
Concomitant swelling and mechanical symptoms, such as locking or catching, suggest loose
OCD fragments.

Patient History
Early presentation often consists of poorly defined symptoms. Patients may report
vague anterior knee pain with intermittent swelling. Approximately 80% of patients with
an OCD lesion report nonspecific knee pain. In addition to pain and swelling, patients
may report of mechanical symptoms, such as catching or locking.19
Physical Examination
Physical examination often elicits tenderness over the area of the OCD lesion, most commonly
the anteromedial aspect of the knee.
Wilson test to detect potential OCD lesion
Internally rotate the tibia while extending the knee from 90° to 30°.
Positive if pain is present with internal rotation and extension that is relieved with external
rotation

Physical Examination
Physical examination findings may correlate with the location of the lesion. Most
commonly, the OCD lesion is along the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle.
Therefore, patients may have tenderness along the medial aspect of the knee. A
thorough knee examination evaluating range of motion and ligamentous stability is
critical to avoid concomitant pathology.19

Imaging Studies
Radiography
Plain radiographs may be used to evaluate patients with knee symptoms and/or signs of an
OCD lesion. Radiographs should include AP, lateral, notch, and patellofemoral views. Notch
and lateral views aid in evaluation of lesion localization and size.

Radiography
Radiographs are first-line imaging studies for patients with OCD lesions. Surgeons must
obtain weight-bearing radiographs and assess the physeal status of the patient. AP and
lateral radiographs usually are insufficient to properly visualize OCD lesions. Tunnel or
notch radiographs can help determine the location of OCD lesions (Figure 16).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may be used to characterize an OCD lesion or to assess for concomitant knee pathology
(Figure 17). MRI provides essential additional information about lesion size, cartilage and
subchondral bone status, signal intensity below the lesion, and the presence of loose bodies.20
MRI staging system for OCD lesions
Stage I: thickening of articular cartilage and low signal changes
Stage II: articular cartilage breached, low signal rim behind fragment
Stage III: articular cartilage breached, high signal changes behind fragment indicating
synovial fluid behind fragment
Stage IV: loose body
Increased signal intensity, cyst formation or fluid below the lesion, and disruption of the
articular cartilage may indicate instability of the OCD lesion.
A stable OCD lesion is defined as one that has not breached the articular cartilage or
subchondral bone-lesion interface.

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonsurgical management is indicated for stable OCD lesions, especially in children or
adolescents with open physes.
Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical management typically involves a period of activity modifications, often with
crutch-protected–weight bearing. This is followed by normal weight-bearing and rehabilitation
exercises.
If clinical or radiographic signs of healing are present after a minimum of 3 to 4 months, then
gradual resumption of rehabilitation can be attempted. This eventually is followed by sports
and impact activities as tolerated.
Nonsurgical management is associated with a success rate of approximately 50% in skeletally
immature OCD patients.
Larger lesion size, skeletal maturity, lesion location other than the medial femoral condyle, and
lesion instability have been correlated with lower success rates in skeletally immature patients
with OCD.
Little evidence supports any particular treatment modality (cast immobilization, brace
management, splinting, an unloader brace, electrical or ultrasonographic bone simulators, or
activity restrictions alone) over another.

Techniques/Procedures
Occasionally, OCD lesions are managed via a trial of nonsurgical management consisting
of activity restrictions. Patients are instructed to cease activity that exacerbates pain. The
goal of nonsurgical management is to allow the osteochondral lesion to heal and to
prevent displacement. Immobilization may include partial–weight bearing with a cast,
hinged knee brace, or crutches. According to American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons clinical practice guidelines, inconclusive evidence supports one nonsurgical
treatment modality over another. No widely accepted rehabilitation protocol exists for
patients with OCD lesions.21 Physical therapy focuses on advancing patients through

various stages of rehabilitation, including passive range of motion, active range of
motion, strengthening, and proprioceptive training. After patients have progressed to
full active motion and strength similar to that of the contralateral leg, they can begin
running, with eventual progression to sport-specific activities. Approximately 50% to 67%
of OCD lesions in skeletally immature patients heal after 6 to 18 months of nonsurgical
management.17
Research has been directed at predicting stable OCD lesions in which nonsurgical
management will fail. Wall et al22 attempted to determine which patient and lesion
characteristics predispose patients to failed nonsurgical treatment. In the study, 47 OCD
lesions in skeletally immature patients were retrospectively reviewed; 34% failed to
respond to a 6-month trial of nonsurgical management. Lesion size was determined to
be the strongest prognostic variable, with a mean size of 208 mm2 in patients in whom
healing occurred versus a mean size of 288 mm2 in patients in whom healing did not
occur. In addition, healing was less likely in patients with mechanical symptoms.
Surgical Management
Indications
Symptomatic skeletally immature patients with salvageable unstable or displaced OCD lesions
Symptomatic skeletally mature patients with salvageable unstable or displaced OCD lesions
Mixed evidence exists on the efficacy of arthroscopic drilling for stable symptomatic OCD
lesions in skeletally immature patients or for stable lesions that did not healed after a 3-month
trial of nonsurgical management.
The objectives of surgical management are maintenance or restoration of joint congruity and
rigid fixation of unstable fragments if they are salvageable.
The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons clinical practice guidelines found weak or
inconclusive support for most OCD-related treatment protocols.21
Consensus exists that surgical treatment be offered to symptomatic skeletally immature and
mature patients with salvageable unstable or displaced OCD lesions.
Inconclusive evidence exits regarding surgical technique.
Consensus exists that patients attend formal physical therapy postoperatively.

Techniques/Procedures
Trans-articular or retro-articular drilling for symptomatic stable OCD lesions can be performed
in skeletally immature patients.
In unstable OCD lesions, any fibrous tissue found at the base of the lesions should be
débrided.
Options for the fixation of unstable fragments that remain relatively intact and congruous
include Herbert screws, cannulated screws, bioabsorbable pins or screws, or osteochondral
transplantation.
Marrow stimulation techniques, such as microfracture, drilling arthroplasty, and abrasion
arthroplasty, are treatment options for OCD lesions smaller than 2 cm in diameter with
minimal bony involvement that are deemed irreparable.
OAT, OCA transplantation, and autogenous chondrocyte implantation also are options for OCD
lesion reconstruction.
Postoperative physical therapy is recommended. Recovery often involves a period of non–
weight bearing or protected–weight bearing while the repaired or reconstructed area heals.
Total recovery typically involves at least 4 to 6 months, after which patients can return to
sports and high-level activities.

Techniques/Procedures
Surgical management usually is indicated in patients in whom nonsurgical treatment
fails and usually begins with arthroscopy. Selection of a surgical treatment option
depends on the stability of the fragment and the integrity of the overlying cartilage.
Surgical management of stable lesions with intact cartilage involves drilling the
subchondral bone, which triggers vascular inflow and may promote re-ossification.
Drilling may consist of trans-articular or retro-articular techniques. Drilling of OCD
lesions tends to be associated with a higher success rate in skeletally immature
patients.19
Unstable lesions with intact cartilage can be approached via various techniques.
Kirschner wires, Herbert screws, cannulated screws, and bioabsorbable implants have
been used. These techniques may require an additional surgical procedure for hardware
removal.19

Salvage procedures are indicated in patients with an unstable lesion with a disrupted
cartilage surface. Several techniques have been described, including ACI, OCA
transplantation, and OAT.19
Few evidence-based recommendations exist regarding rehabilitation after surgical
management of OCD lesions. Four to 12 weeks of non–weight bearing typically is
recommended. Full range of motion is allowed early in the recovery period. A valgus
unloader brace may be beneficial in patients with medial compartment pathology. The
goal of the initial postoperative period is to regain motion, maintain quadriceps function,
and minimize swelling. After the patient has attained full motion and is bearing weight as
tolerated, usually at 3 months postoperatively, strengthening begins. A staged running
program can be initiated approximately 4 to 6 months postoperatively. Patients usually
can return to sport-specific activities after 6 months postoperatively.17
